chain.g: to buffet about, agitate, toss; to sift or winnow

ety.text: From Middle English tossen (“to buffet about, agitate, toss; to sift or winnow”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Old Norse (compare dialectal Norwegian tossa, dialectal Swedish tossa (“to strew, spread”)), or perhaps from an alteration of Middle English tosen (“to tease, pull apart, shred; to wound, injure”). Compare also Dutch tassen (“to pile or heap up, stack”). The Welsh tos (“a quick jerk”) and tosio (“to jerk, toss”) are probably borrowed from the English.

senses.d: A throw, a lob, of a ball etc., with an initial upward direction, particularly with a lack of care.
The coin toss before a cricket match in order to decide who bats first, or before a football match in order to decide the direction of play.
A haughty throwing up of the head.

ex: I don't give a toss about her.
This put us at the board into a Tosse.
"We are all in a toss, in our neighborhood," said Mistress Pottle.

senses.d: A handover from one presenter to another, announced by the first presenter.
ex: The introduction would still be done by the Monitor host in New York's Studio 5B, followed by the toss to the newsperson in Washington.
Then I look again at this message. What a load of toss.
'You were,' John said, with infinite love, 'talking such absolute toss.'
And Uncle Frank is having a wank, And Auntie Floss is having a toss, With Grandad.
Men don't chat about having a toss. We just don't. It's not comfortable.

senses.d: To throw with an initial upward direction.
To lift with a sudden or violent motion.
ex:
He tossed his arm aloft, and proudly told me,
 He would not stay.

Calm region once,
 And full of peace, now tossed and turbulent.

senses.d: To subject to trials; to harass.
ex: Whom devils fly, thus is he tossed of men.

senses.d: To flip a coin, to decide a point of contention.

ex: I don't need it any more; you can just toss it.
to toss a salad; a tossed salad.

senses.d: To search (a room or a cell), sometimes leaving visible disorder, as for valuables or evidence of a crime.
ex: Rankin and Willingham, when they tossed his cell, they took Polaroids so they could get everything back in place.

senses.d: To roll and tumble; to be in violent commotion.
ex: tossing and turning in bed, unable to sleep

ety.text: From mistura (“mixture”) + -ar (forms infinitives), from Latin mīxtura, feminine participle of misceō (“to mix”), from Proto-Indo-European *meiǵ-, *meiḱ- (“to mix”). Alternatively from Old Galician-Portuguese mesturar, from a Late Latin mixturāre, from Latin mīxtura. Compare Italian misturare, archaic Spanish mesturar.
